headline: Rejected the Sapienza-Kantor budget and a tax cap override, leaving the FY2027 city budget resolutions tabled for further negotiation.
summary: The board heard extensive public comment on the city and school budgets and whether to override the municipal tax cap. After debate, aldermen voted down the Sapienza-Kantor budget and a motion to override the tax cap, then tabled all FY2027 budget resolutions for continued work. The board also approved routine consent agenda items, two staff retirements, board appointments, a lien subordination, a special education funding transfer, and several staffing and ordinance changes.
decisions: Approved the consent agenda, including the May 19 minutes, sidewalk petitions, committee reports, and a new Welfare Reserve Account ordinance amendment.
Accepted with regret the retirement of Assessor Lee Ann Provencher, effective July 31, 2026.
Accepted with regret the retirement of Library Director Denise van Zanten, effective August 1, 2026.
Confirmed nominations to the Lead Exposure Prevention Commission and the Conservation Commission.
Approved the warrant for unlicensed dogs to be committed to the Chief of Police.
Approved subordination of the city's lien on the property at 31 Central Street.
Approved transferring about $1 million in excess revenues to the Special Education Trust and using about $1 million from the Teaching and Learning Trust to cover a special education shortfall.
Approved Water Works Department staffing changes recommended by the Human Resources/Insurance Committee.
Approved Police Department staffing reclassifications recommended by the Human Resources/Insurance Committee.
Approved a $25,000 budget authorization for a Community Improvement Program UPS project and referred it to the Finance Committee.
Suspended the board's rules and ordained on third reading an ordinance amendment changing the Lead Exposure Prevention Commission's composition.
Ordained an ordinance creating a Welfare Reserve Account.
Referred to the Administration/Information Systems Committee a review of disabled and elderly tax exemptions, with intent to increase them.
Rejected the Sapienza-Kantor Fiscal Year 2027 budget by a 2-12 roll call vote.
Rejected a motion to override the city charter's tax cap provision for the budget by a 9-5 roll call vote.
Tabled the Fiscal Year 2027 budget resolutions for further negotiation.

## BOARD OF MAYOR AND ALDERMEN

June 2, 2026 at 7:00 PM

Mayor Ruais called the meeting to order.

Mayor Ruais called for the Pledge of Allegiance; this function being led by Alderman Dexter.

A moment of silence was observed.

The Clerk called the roll.

Present: Aldermen Kaw-uh, Goonan, Dexter, Fajardo, Bonilla, Kantor, Trisciani, O’Neil, Terrio, Sapienza, Burkush, Barry, Vincent, Thomas

Mayor Ruais: With the board's indulgence, I have one recognition I would like to make this evening with the folks from Engine Five. I have the distinct privilege of recognizing their heroic actions on March 27th. City of Manchester, a Resolution: Whereas on March 27, 2026, members of the Manchester Fire Department's Engine Five responded to an unknown medical call that was updated in route to a cardiac arrest emergency. And whereas upon arrival, engine five personnel found a patient who was not breathing and without a pulse requiring immediate lifesaving intervention. And whereas the crew promptly initiated high quality CPR and utilized a 911 language interpreter to effectively communicate with Spanish speaking bystanders and the patient's family. And whereas engine five members connected the patient to a 12-lead cardiac monitor and successfully administered two defibrillations while continuing advanced resuscitative efforts. And whereas AMR ALS one personnel arrived on scene and worked alongside engine five to provide continued advanced life support measures in a coordinated and professional manner. And whereas, through the extraordinary skill, dedication, teamwork and commitment to public service demonstrated by Lieutenant Carl Ludwig, firefighter John Amin, firefighter John Berry, firefighter Thomas Welch, paramedic Dave Rideout and EMT Kieran Remillard, the patient was successfully transported to Catholic Medical Center with a restored pulse and breathing independently. And whereas this successful outcome exemplifies the professionalism, training, compassion and teamwork displayed each day by the members of the Manchester Fire Department and American Medical Response in service to the residents of Manchester. Now, therefore, I, Jay Ruais, Mayor of the City of Manchester, New Hampshire, do hereby recognize and commend Lieutenant Carl

- Ludwig, firefighter John Amin, firefighter John Berry, firefighter Thomas Welch, paramedic

Dave Rideout and EMT Kieran Remillard for their outstanding actions, dedication to duty and lifesaving efforts on March 27, 2026 and extend the gratitude and appreciation of the City of Manchester for their exemplary service to our community. Thank you, gentlemen, very much.

PUBLIC COMMENT

1. Mayor Ruais advised that the purpose of the public comment session is to give residents of Manchester the opportunity to address the Board. All people wishing to speak must sign up with their name, address and topic. Once called, they will have up to three minutes to speak and any comments must be directed to the chair and concluded when their time is up. If the Clerk calls their name and they are not present to speak, they will not be given a second opportunity. Any

resident wishing to speak will come forward to the nearest microphone, clearly state their name and address when recognized and give their comments.

Ann Williams, 151 Rosegate Farm Drive: I'm a fixed income retiree and ward eight voter. I'm here in favor of the original proposed alternative budget, the one that helps Manchester in its goal to be that best mid-sized city. I represent more of ward eight than you may think. Surprised? Our demographics are changing. The building of many new apartments and condos have brought young families and young professionals who have an increased need for services. I can support this sentiment with the numbers from the recent election, where our alderman won by only 26 votes. Board members serving 8 to 10 years and sometimes more than a decade, it may be time to make room for new voices and fresh perspectives. Manchester's future belongs to the next generation. Younger residents deserve the opportunity to help shape the city they will inherit. I am concerned that a singular focus on avoiding new taxes or tax cap compliance does not create a sustainable, livable and thriving Manchester. In fact, it risks taking the city backward. Remember what Manchester looked like in the 80s and 90s before the airport expansion, before restaurants lined Elm Street, before Delta Dental Stadium, and before the arena that now brings concerts, sporting events and entertainment to our community? We chose to make investments to transform Manchester into a city we are proud of. At the very least, we should be maintaining what we have while continuing to move forward, not backward. The school budget appears to be at the heart of our consternation. The naysayers talk about how reduced enrollment must translate to reduced budget. Honestly, if you've had kids graduate and leave your home, did your costs go down? Are you paying less for food, for insurance, for anything? It is deeply unfair for some yelling the loudest: a Concord legislator, past aldermen, current aldermen, who have chosen private education for their own children, to criticize public school spending while denying public school students the same opportunities and resources as their kids have. Families who rely on public schools deserve strong support and investment, not continued cuts. And you heard me right. Some of the loudest voices you've heard recently have sent or are sending their kids to private schools. Another seemingly small budget cut, but one packed with significance, is the plan to eliminate the of role the budget for identifying and writing grants. A serious mistake. As this area has the expertise to secure outside funding for Manchester. If you are headstrong into cutting department budgets, grants will be a lifeline. I urge the vote to the board to vote to fund our critical public service departments, even if it means going above the tax cap.

Harrison Williams, 639 N Bay Street: I speak before you to address a critical issue impacting the very foundation of our city's well-being, our budget and the tax cap. I understand that overriding the tax cap is a significant decision, one that requires careful consideration. However, I urge you to set aside any hesitation and recognize the urgent need to address our financial framework to meet the rising demands of our community. We are facing a perfect storm of rising costs. Our schools are striving to provide the best possible education for our children, but their budgets are stretched thin. A robust education system is not a luxury. It is an investment in our future, and it demands adequate funding. Similarly, ensuring the safety and security of our citizens requires a fair and competitive police force. Again, this requires funding. We cannot compromise on the resources needed to support our law enforcement. Do not sit there and claim to support the police if you are not going to provide them the resources to perform their jobs. Beyond these vital areas, our city's infrastructure from the Departments of Public Works and basic road maintenance is showing its age. These are not optional services. They are essential for a thriving community. Neglecting them now will lead to far more costly repairs and potential crises down the road. How can we hope to be a great city if we don't invest in ourselves? How can anyone hope to succeed if they're not willing to believe in themselves? The current tax cap, while well-intentioned, is now acting as a constraint, a noose, effectively strangling our ability to adequately fund those crucial services. We are essentially battling a rising tide with a shrinking bucket. The same dollar no longer buys the things it once could. The cost of everything from groceries to gas increases, compounding on itself. Our tax dollars simply don't stretch as far as they used to. Ignoring the fundamental decrease in purchasing power is a huge misunderstanding of how the economy works. As someone who has watched this board repeatedly struggle with this issue, I would be so bold as to implore the city to adjust or even abolish the tax cap. This may be daunting, but it is becoming an increasingly necessary step to ensure we can adequately address the rising costs of providing essential services that this city offers. It's about recognizing the value of our city's future and investing in its long-term health. Let's not allow budgetary constraints to compromise the quality of life for our residents. Let us be bold, proactive and responsible in securing a sustainable and thriving future for our city.

Richard Irving, Ward 2: Before celebrating Manchester's 180th birthday, please protect the tax cap, because you're on the verge of voting on a budget that will raise property taxes. City government wasn't created to be a charity. I'm asking the mayor and aldermen to stop spending our money foolishly on personal wants, like new schools and replacement sidewalks near the theater district on Hanover Street. Focus on your city's needs like housing, roads, health, police, parks and recreation, clearing of snow and ice on all sidewalks and trails for everyone, and helping the homeless population. And finally, on that subject, we won't tolerate homelessness and bad behavior on the part of vagrants that break the law and disrespect our city and its taxpayers, and not about citizens living and paying bills.

Paul LaFerriere 185 Eastern Avenue: I'm addressing statements made at the last Board of Mayor and Aldermen meeting about the budget proposed by Alderman Trisciani and Burkush to override Manchester's tax cap. It is unacceptable that board members implied that anyone who opposes that budget somehow does not support the Manchester Police Department or back the blue. Frankly, mayor, I found those accusations extremely offensive. I, along with other ward four members, couldn't make it and demand a public apology from those aldermen that stated this, and they know who they are. Your honor, as you know, I'm a retired disabled Army veteran and retired federal law enforcement officer, and I'll always support our Manchester PD. Many taxpayers oppose the wasteful school and city budget. It should be reworked with savings redirected to secure approval of the Manchester Police contract and fund DPW repairs to sidewalks, roads and infrastructure. Because I am a constituent who spoke against this budget at the last meeting, we were offended by public comments claiming that we do not support them. Well, we Republicans and the Republican aldermen who were accused deserve a public apology in this chamber or the matter should be addressed through the city's core values and policy procedures. The aldermen who opposed this tax cap override listened to the taxpayers and are presenting two alternative budgets tonight. The issue was never whether our police department deserves better pay and support. It does. The real issue is that the Democratic alderman used the police contract as cover for a much larger spending increase that could be shortchanged that contract. Residents can see the difference. Another alderman wrote a letter to the union leader accusing the taxpayers of threatening a Republican alderman over the Democratic budget proposal. That

accusation is wrong. Taxpayers are doing exactly what citizens are supposed to do in a democracy: using their First Amendment rights to speak out about a budget that affects their families, homes and future. To the Mayor and Aldermen, you were elected by the people and you work for all the people of Manchester. That means listening to all residents, not just those that agree with you. At least the Republican aldermen listened to the taxpayers and responded by offering alternatives. I did not hear a Democratic alderman do the same. Instead, I continue to hear to support their budget that many residents oppose. That is why tabling it was the right outcome for the last meeting. The alderman who made that accusation owes taxpayers a written public apology to the Union Leader. Political theatrics are not needed. As I said before, senior citizens and taxpayers cannot afford a property tax increase, renters cannot afford higher housing costs driven by rising property taxes. If taxes rise, more residents will face financial hardship and housing instability.

Arnold Mikolo, 73 Clinton Street: I'm here as somebody who cares deeply about the future of our city and public space in green infrastructure. I'm urging to include $250,000 for urban forestry site preparation for this year's capital improvement plan. This isn’t a new idea or untested proposal. The city has already done the hard work of securing the USDA Urban Forestry Grant. The grant represents a real commitment from the federal government to help us grow our tree canopy, but federal grants don't operate in a vacuum. They require matching infrastructure, local investments, and implementation capacity. The sidewalk bump outs this funding will support are what makes tree planting physically possible in dense, heavily paved areas in our city. Think of some of our corridor blocks where there is nothing but concrete from building to curb. There is no soil, no space, no room for trees to take root without first removing hardscape and creating a dedicated planting zone. That's exactly what this funding does. It doesn't replicate the grants. It activates it. Without the $250,000, we leave those federal dollars underutilized. We lose planting season. We can never get it back, and we send a message to the agencies and organizations investing in our cities that we are not ready to meet them halfway. I know this board takes its budget responsibility seriously. I'm asking you tonight to take this opportunity seriously, too. The groundwork has been laid. The grant is secure. All that's missing is your vote to fund the infrastructure that makes it real. Please include this in your CIP.

Rick Blais, 733 Chestnut Street: A lot of people talked tonight, so I'll just read through. I want to thank you guys. I see so much commonality here. There are threads dividing people. It's not valleys, it's not rivers. But we all want great schools, safe neighborhoods, strong infrastructure response, responsible spending. Because at this point, it's getting outrageous what's happening, over the years. About two years ago or three years ago, the Board of Mayor and Aldermen at that time had voted into giving the school taxing power versus the aldermen and mayor, and with no more oversight for the mayor being on that board. I made a proposal at that time saying, because nothing can get done in two years, you all know that, I keep hearing that over and over again. You run for election, you win, then you spend a year voting on real stuff. And then the second year you have to spend massaging the voters and trying to meet that person in the middle. As a result, nothing gets done. And that's the challenge. Nobody can work a long-term plan to change the way the city is operating. We operate problem to problem, rather than more strategic planning. As far as the school budget continuing to increase every year after year, I hear people saying cut. I haven't heard the school getting a cut budget from the year before. Now they're talking making a proposal and that proposed budget is getting cut, it has nothing to do with the real money that's being spent. So that's something that I think people play with words to stir the emotions of people up. And it's sad that they have to do that. Too often when a budget reduction is discussed, immediately it shifts to laying off teachers. Like I said at the last hearing I was at, they never talk about the bloat in the administration. There's 30%, I guarantee you can cut from there with AI and more efficiencies. But they choose to ignore that and they always go to the teachers. Why? It's the heartstrings of Manchester. The kids are going to suffer. Well, maybe the administration needs to suffer a little more. So, I'm a firm believer in that. I think we should have a detailed line-item budget. When I look at a budget and this is big number, if I'm an average taxpayer, I have no clue what I'm looking at. Well, fortunately I know what to look for in a budget, but when you have a line item you can make honest cuts. Without those line items there, nothing gets cut. They smoke and mirrors the numbers that they give us, so it's very dangerous. The Manchester School District is at the bottom of the state. I don't know about a quality education, but I know you can go to Trinity for $15,000 and get a superior education versus $20,000 plus per student that we're paying. So, for them to say that their kids are getting a great education, it isn't. Kids that are graduating and going to college, they have to spend an extra year in their program, whether it's a four year, they have to go five just to get the remedial math and English done. That's sad because we're letting down every high school kid in this city.

Guy Ouellette, Ward 6: There are two constants in life: death and taxes. I oppose any tax increase. For those of us who are fortunate enough to be retired or soon to be retired, the tax burden is overwhelming. We've been good stewards of the Queen City for generations and decades. We are trying, and I want to emphasize trying, to enjoy our golden years with less stress and worry. Now with inflation, food, gas, meds, just to name a few, our disposable income has all but vanished. We sacrifice one for the other. Increasing the tax cap would only create more anxiety and mental duress, which is a benefit to no one, but it will create more concerns down the road. We need to recognize and appreciate what our elders have accomplished and done through their lives in the city. We've built new athletic fields throughout the city, new municipal buildings, dog parks, etc.. When is enough going to be enough? Increasing the cap will have an irreversible adverse effect on us all. How much can we sacrifice our overall health? Our happiness is at stake. We are taxing our elders out of their domiciles. It's un-American and a sad narrative to put forth. We are better than that. Driving around the city, there are real estate signs going up everywhere. Why? Affordability. Quality of life. We don't need to mistreat our elders and put them on the streets. They've already made and paid their dues. They don't deserve to be treated like this. Please, I implore you to show some good judgment and compassion. Vote no on the increase of the cap. And I want to expressly thank all of our service members in the audience this evening for their service. I also want to thank the Manchester Police Department and our firefighters for everything they do.

Cindy Stewart, 255 Sagamore Street: I am an at large member of the Board of School Committee. I am speaking directly to the Manchester taxpayers. There is a wave of misinformation circulating in our community. I do not know how the Manchester School District became the bogeyman to some, but tonight, on behalf of the 12,000 children we serve, I want to set the record straight. First, our financials are an open and a verified book. The recent audit from the independent auditing firm gave the district a clean opinion with explicit praise. Any insinuation of inaccurate or altered financial statements is blatantly false. If anyone has fictitious accusations to levy, please take them up directly with the auditor. Second, we are absorbing decades of broken federal promises. When the IDEA Act was enacted in 1975, Congress committed to funding 40% of the per pupil cost for special education. In 51 years, that federal share has never topped 17%. Liability passes straight to the municipalities, with special ed costs increase exponentially. The result? A current annual shortfall to this district of $10 million. Third, by state law, this district must provide transportation for Manchester students attending parochial, private, and charter schools within city routes. We receive zero reimbursement from those institutions, and we bear 100% of the cost. If school transportation is cut in the budget, the impact will be felt by every single family with school age children in Manchester. Furthermore, we provide most special ed services to Manchester's parochial and charter school students. This means district staff and contract workers are deployed to or housed within these institutions because reimbursements rarely cover the full cost. Many Manchester taxpayers subsidize the difference. Fourth, New Hampshire's base adequacy funding is embarrassingly the lowest in the nation. To add insult to injury, Manchester is the only municipality in New Hampshire that funds its public schools at less than 50% of the municipal budget. When we talk about the school budget, we are not talking about reckless spending. We are talking about navigating a minefield of unfunded mandates and intentional downshifting of costs to the local level. The villainization of our teachers, administrators, and especially our students, is unfounded. No one is coming to save our city, not Washington and certainly not Concord. It is up to us; or more accurately, it is up to you.

Kelly Jobel: I'm a district employee here in Manchester. I'm here tonight to speak in support of what is best for our children as a district employee of 25 years, having experience at both the school and district level. Today, while I was helping a middle school student with their computer, I asked the student if they were excited for summer. The student quickly responded no, followed by several reasons. They would miss school over the summer. For so many of our students, school is the only constant, safe place in their lives and they look forward to coming to school each day. I'm sure many of you can relate to seeing the crazy increases on your favorite items at the grocery store. In December of 2020, this gallon of orange juice from Walmart was $6.97. Today, the same gallon of orange juice is $11.53. Our schools are facing the same issue. This toner cartridge costs $42 more than it cost in 2023, over a 30% increase in just three years. This cartridge is only one example of one product out of thousands of products and services the district purchases and uses each year to provide our students with the best education they deserve in addition to many products that were free for educational institutions that are now charging for them. As you make your decision tonight, please support a budget that supports our schools and providing what is best for our students.

Greg Erskine, 125 Electric Street: I am here to speak in favor of the budget that was recently proposed by Miss Trisciani and because I'm a product of Manchester's public schools, K through 12. I started kindergarten at Smyth Road, then seventh and eighth grade at Hillside, then High School at Central. I did alright in school. I took the highest- level classes I could, and I got into a good college because of Manchester. At college, I was surrounded by kids who attended private schools, and what I noticed when I got there from Manchester was that I did not know any less than they did. I did not struggle any more than they did. I not did not perform any more poorly than they did, and it was because of the hard work of teachers here in Manchester. That kind of difficult educational labor was possible because of a teacher to student ratio that kept our class sizes at reasonable levels, and that kept support staff hired to make sure that our schools run smoothly. With the proper amount of funding our schools can be and have been the equal of any other school in the nation, public or private. Manchester can be a gem among public school systems nationwide. A properly funded school system is the keystone on which the virtue of our civil society is built. But beyond this loftiness, the other thing I remember about being a teenager is that occasionally they get into trouble around Manchester. I look back on this now because I'm now a father. I've got four kids in Manchester's public schools just like I was, they're young, but I know that as they get older, they're more likely to get into things they probably shouldn't. A public school system that keeps kids engaged at every level is an investment. It means that down the road, we will have to spend less money on public safety because as our kids become teens, they will feel the spiritual fulfillment of education instead of getting bored or stupid or rascally. It's also an investment in the long-term health of Manchester, because it means that when my kids decide to have families, they are likely to settle down and do so in Manchester, just as I have, just as my parents did, just as my grandparents did, because they know that Manchester made them strong and they will return to pay that strength back to the city that we all love. Every day I drop my kids off at Northwest Elementary and our family thinks it's an incredible place that's full of teachers and administrators and support staff that are so dedicated, so sharp, and experienced and compassionate. Every day I am filled with gratitude for the education that my kids are getting. I would like to maintain that level of excellence for the rest of their schooling and for everyone in Manchester.

Jessica Margeson: I want to speak tonight about timing because I think timing is everything when it comes to the $250,000 urban forestry infrastructure request. Budget season involves competing priorities, and I understand that everyone in this room understands that there are roads to fix, buildings to maintain, a lot of potholes to fill, services to fund, and only so many dollars to go around. I'm not here to suggest that this allocation is the only important one, but I am here to make the case that this particular investment has a window, and if we miss it, we may not get it back. The city has secured a USDA Urban Forestry grant. That grant was not easy to get. It required applications, planning, community engagement events and a demonstrated commitment to canopy expansion. That work is done. The federal commitment is in place. Mayor, what we need now is the local infrastructure investment that allows us to actually use it. The curb bump outs, the hardscape removal, the site alterations, that turn a grant award into trees in the ground and an investment in our inner city. If this board does not include the $250,000 in this year's CIP, we risk falling behind on implementation timelines tied to the grant. We risk losing planting seasons. We risk sending a signal to federal partners that the city cannot follow through on its commitments, and we risk watching a rare funding opportunity slowly expire while our most vulnerable neighborhoods remain unshaded. Parks and recreation brought forward a sound proposal. The mayor's budget didn't include it, but the board has the final word on CIP, and I'm asking you to use that authority to add this back in. The grant is there. The plan is there. The community need is there. Please make the funding there, too. I want to add, my biggest question, I get asked about how it helps with the heat canopy. There's a period of time in our city where a lot of trees in that area were taken down, and those trees provided shade to housing, which cuts down on the electricity use to cool that housing in the summertime. And it can get quite hot in the sun.

Maria Matesi: I'm here tonight because I care deeply about the future of the city and the opportunities we have to create for people who live in Manchester. As you consider this year's budget, I ask that you support the community first budget that was presented here on May 19th by nine aldermen. Also include the $250,000 investment for the streets and tree bumps. When I think about what makes a community strong, I think about two things. Opportunities; opportunities we provide for children and the environment we create for families to thrive in. That is why investing in our schools is so important. Our students deserve every chance to succeed in the schools. The community first budget would restore critical budgeting to the school district and also help with the programs of summer and also for transportation. Nelson Mandela once said, education is the most powerful weapon which you could use to change the world. And I believe that is true. Every dollar we invest in education is an investment in the future of Manchester and also for the next generation, teachers and health care, and the list goes on. I want to ask you guys something. If we didn't have the school system that we had before, would we all be sitting here today? About two years ago, we had a great district that gave us everything. The teachers were funded, buses, summer programs were funded, and students were

thriving. And now everybody's scared of what's going to be happening in the next few summers that are coming. I would suggest that we take our education seriously when it comes to funding. Our educators deserve more support when it comes to school systems. Students are struggling to focus on outcomes because we don't have enough of a support system. I ask that we provide more support with the budgeting, and also, I know there's more problems that we have to focus on, but there is always more to offer when it comes to the school system. Lastly, I would ask that we really think about these budgeting things when it comes to school system. Our students need help, our educators need help. And also, the roads; please, the roads, when it comes to winter it's really hard to get around. This year it was really bad and I pray that next time we can do better with budgeting on that part, too.

Amber Nicole Cannan, Ward 3: I'm a Manchester resident and a person with disabilities and a DPW commissioner. I walk these streets. I've been hit by cars while crossing them on sidewalks. That's why I care about bump outs. When we talk about trees, we often talk about environmental benefits and those are important. Trees improve air quality, reduce heat, and make neighborhoods healthier. But I'd like to speak about this from a disability perspective. Shade is an accessibility tool for many people with disabilities, older adults, people with heart conditions, respiratory conditions, mobility impairments, or heat sensitivity. Excessive heat can make walking through the city difficult or even dangerous. The neighborhoods targeted by this project are some of the most paved parts of Manchester, and I'm talking about those bump outs for the trees. They are exactly the places where people need relief from heat the most. The challenge is that in many of these locations, there simply is not enough green space to plant the trees without creating the infrastructure to support them. That's why the bump outs matter. The trees and the bump outs kind of go together, and the bump outs provide benefits beyond trees themselves. They shorten crossing distances, they calm traffic. It's a really big one. They make pedestrians more visible. Another really big one. They create safer crossings for children, older adults, wheelchair users and anyone who moves through the city at a slower pace like me. Over the last few weeks, many of us have spent time talking about participation in our community and what it means for people to feel welcome in public spaces. I would argue that participation starts long before someone walks into City Hall. It starts with whether they can safely cross the street, reach a bus stop, get to a park or parking spot, visit a business or travel through their neighborhood with dignity and independence. The physical design of our city sends a message about who belongs here. Investments like these send the message that Manchester is a city built for everyone. This is one of those rare investments that improves accessibility, public health, pedestrian safety, neighborhood quality of life, and environmental outcomes all at the same time. I hope you will support the funding and help make sure these trees can be planted where they are needed the most.

Shams Muldad, 287 Weston Road: I'm here in support of the community first budget. I would like to first thank you all for your time, your hard work on the school budget, and listening to students. I appreciate the opportunity to share my perspective and hope you will consider my thoughts on the budget proposals. I think many of us are familiar with the condition of our roads. Whenever my dad and I drive to my clubs and activities, we can't help but notice and feel the potholes along the way. They are frustrating for drivers and passengers alike, and I know many other residents share those same concerns. I would also like to highlight the importance of the West Side Library. The community first budget proposal will allow us to keep it open, which is especially important for the many students and families who rely on it for educational resources and internet access in a safe place to learn. Removing the West Side Library would take away those opportunities. This is why I support the community first budget. It accommodates the needs of our city and makes it a better place for everyone.

Yaniel Aponte, 307 Merrimack Street: I am in support of the Community First Budget because I know firsthand, as many of you do, about the bad roads. Every day I take the bus from Central to MST and I sit near the middle or I sit closer to the back. Every time I sit closer to the back, I hit many bumps and I basically fly out of my seat. Recently I was sitting near the back away from people so I can relax after a long three hours of doing hair, and I watch a video while I make it to my class. I was sitting at the back, unknowing of what would happen, and then our bus hit a huge pothole. I flew up into the air and back down to my seat. Startled, I spilled my water everywhere. I know this might not seem like the biggest issue, but if it were anyone else or a disabled student in a wheelchair in the bus, if they hit the pothole, they could have been seriously injured. Picture yourself every day on your way to work or class. You're driving or getting driven. You have to go past the potholes every day. At some point, it could damage your car, your tires, and somehow your engine. I believe if you endorse the community first budget, they will put money towards fixing the roads, making your ride to work, school or ride back home much simpler. I ask that you listen to our young voices and vote for the community first budget. George Kalipolites, 668 Lake Avenue: There's a handout being passed out and it's really simple. It's about the property taxes. If you go up 12%, the handout will show a 12% increase on a $420,000 home. At $8,400, it'll go up to $9,008. That's an increase of over $1,000. People can't afford this increase. Foreclosures are up 24% from last year. Bankruptcies are up 42% from last year nationally. If the aldermen care, vote no and stay with the tax cap.

Lou D'Allesandro, 332 Saint James Avenue: I've lived in the same house for 55 years. I pay my taxes every year. All of my children went to the Manchester public school system, K through 12. The people of the City of Manchester and the State of New Hampshire have invested in me for 50 years, sending me to public office. I served in the New Hampshire State Senate for 26 years. I chaired the Finance Committee in the Senate on three occasions. I chaired the Ways and Means Committee on three occasions. We should be angry at the State of New Hampshire for screwing the people of Manchester by eliminating funding. By eliminating the interest and dividends tax, $340 million was returned to the wealthiest people in the state and withheld from those in need. When you reduce funding from the state, you reduce funding to the city and the towns. The State of New Hampshire has withheld municipal aid for 20 years. We were supposed to be part of revenue sharing. If the state ever paid the revenue sharing that they owe the City of Manchester, we would be loaded with money. So, I ask you, the Board of Mayor and Aldermen, to invest in the citizens of the state and invest in our students in public education. The greatest gift that can be given to any human being is a quality public education. Think of it; we are one of the few nations in the world that offers a free and appropriate public education to its population. How could we deny that to our children? Many people sitting around this room, aldermen, you are products of public education. You went through the system. You received the benefits of the system. And indeed, you should be supplying those benefits to the children who are in our schools today. We have the most diversified population in the State of New Hampshire. Diversification is the essence of success. Diversity and culture bring us together and ingratiates us. So, I ask you, the Board of Mayor and Aldermen, to be responsive, to invest in people. Investment produces dividends. Dividends are the people who stay in Manchester, the people who work in Manchester, and the people who strive to make Manchester a better place. You have that responsibility. Please live up to it.

Nancy Troupakis, Karatzas Avenue: Let's be honest about what this vote is. Tonight, you are deciding whether to respect the 3% tax cap or to push it far beyond to roughly 12%. That's not a small increase. That's a significant expansion of the tax burden on every resident in this city. The tax cap exists to protect taxpayers, and it only gets broken if this board chooses to break it. Many of you spoke about fiscal responsibility and protecting taxpayers during your campaigns. Tonight is where those words are tested. Your credibility is at stake because this vote is where commitment either holds or it doesn't. I want you to think about the people you represent and their own household budgets. People are not seeing 12% increases in their income. Families are stretched. Yet this proposal asks them to absorb far more than they would ever experience. So, the question is simple. Why are taxpayers being asked to pay more when there isn't stronger accountability for how the money is being spent? We have declining enrollment. We have unacceptable test outcomes. And yet, where is the pushback? Where is the accountability before asking residents to pay more? Because right now the burden is being placed on the taxpayer; it should be placed instead on the system to improve. Also, I want to address something. Many residents are hearing there is a growing concern that some who campaigned on protecting the tax cap may be prepared to vote to override it tonight. If that's not true, this is your opportunity to make that clear. But if it is, that is exactly how trust is broken. Because those votes were commitments, the voters relied on it. And if you vote to override this cap, you are choosing to pass that burden directly onto the residents. If I could leave with one thing tonight, this is a line in the sand. You either respect the tax cap or you break it. There is no middle ground. Many of you made clear promises to the to the people of this city that you would protect them exactly from this kind of decision. So, let's not dress this up. If you vote to override this tax cap tonight, you are breaking that promise, plain and simple. And you are forcing taxpayers to carry that burden that you are elected to protect them from. Call it whatever you want, but that's what it is. And here's a reality: when election time comes November of 2027, it won't be about explanations. It won't be about process. It will be about who kept their word and who didn't hold the line or be prepared to answer for it.

Mackenzie Verdiner, 181 Wilson Street: I'm 20 years old. I'm a voter. I rent an apartment here in Manchester. One thing I noticed about my community is that a majority of my neighbors don't own the property that they live on. We rent it. When in conversation with aldermen and I have conversations with you all very often, I hear that we need to protect the taxpayer. But my question is, what is the percent of people who own property in Manchester that actually live here? As anecdotal evidence, I can tell you that all of the landlords that I have had did not live in Manchester. They lived in Massachusetts. So, the last few years, when you voted for a budget that fell under the tax cap, you're protecting people who don't drive on our roads, who don't send their children to schools, and who aren't going to call our police department. I did some research to try and find a number to support my theory that the majority of Manchester property owners do not live in Manchester, and there wasn't any data that showed the number of absentee landlords. But I did find that 35.7% of Manchester housing is detached single family homes, while 59.5% of Manchester housing consists of buildings with 3 to 50 units, showing that there are more renters than homeowners. When you're considering your decision on the budget, I urge you to consider a utilitarian philosophy. What will help the most amount of people? If most people in Manchester are renters trying to make ends meet, then vote for a budget that helps their children get to school, not one that means that their kids will have to walk two miles to get to school. Vote for a budget that makes our roads safe to drive on. I don't want to have to swerve every day to work just to avoid the potholes. I want you to protect the people that live here, not just the people that own property here. As a young person, as a taxpayer, and as a renter, I want you to know that I'm willing to pay a few extra dollars more in rent if it means that our community is taken care of. I'm in support of a community first budget, and I hope that you are, too.

Robert Sternberg, Ward 2: Both our children went to schools in Manchester, at Smyth Road, Hillside, and Central High School, and they're both doing very well. Thankfully, they don't live in the basement. I just want to emphasize the importance of the education department and the education that our children are receiving in Manchester. I want to also point out, as has been pointed out before, the condition of our roads is terrible. And I also want to point out that we support the Manchester Police Department and the Manchester Fire Department, and that's all I want to say. But the important thing is for the Board of Aldermen to come up with a budget that supports all these factors and that takes into account the tax burden as well.

Carol Sternberg, Ward 2: As my husband said, we have two children who are doing very well and who went to Manchester public schools, and we were very happy with their progress through the years. This community first budget might add something to the school system. Obviously, it's going to add some money that we'll all have to be contributing to. But I think education is so important. And I also feel very strongly that our streets, our roads, our sidewalks, very much need to be repaired. You would think you were driving in the country and you're driving in Manchester. And I also feel very strongly that we need to keep that West Side Library going.

Stephen Light, Ward 10: I am a Ward ten resident since 1988. For nearly 20 years now, due to neurological disease that left me unable to drive, I have relied solely, almost solely, on the MTA system to get around for work, medical appointments, various other shopping needs, and having done that on a nearly daily basis, I've seen dozens and hundreds of people probably who are in the same situation that I'm in, or a lot worse. I see people with walkers. I see people in wheelchairs on the buses on a daily basis. They need to be able to get around. They need to have the quality of life that we deserve. This has been an issue for many years in this city. As far as budget cuts to our MTA, it's time we all sit down and figure out a good plan, a logical plan to end this problem in our city and help people regain a better quality of life.

Jeff Kassel, 22 Appleton Street: Is it just me, or is it hard to hear what people are saying? Can everybody hear me back there? Okay, maybe I'm getting a little hard of hearing. I'm old. I actually was Donald Trump's classmate in 1966. Not that I voted for him, I didn't, but I want to take you down memory lane. Around 20 years ago, I was the chairman of the Tax Association in Manchester, and we embarked on an effort to promote a spending cap, not a tax cap, because it was very difficult to cap taxes, but a spending cap. I hardly recognized him. And he now works for a lobbying agency that promotes big oil and big gas. I wish I had that job. I'd have a better chance of paying my property taxes, but to go down memory lane, if you remember, when you were in school, there was a teacher that would lecture you in front of the classroom. And we would do it, but we really preferred it when there was a movie or even a film strip that we could watch to break up the monotony, because it's kind of a boring model, a teacher in front of a classroom. I used to be one, but now I'm old and I'm retired, and I don't think we should be spending a quarter of $1 billion on education.

Nikki Beaulieu, Ward 6: I am here to speak against overriding the tax cap and yet another property tax increase in the City of Manchester. I have owned two properties in Manchester since 2008. I now live in ward six. From 2023 to 2025 alone, I paid the city nearly $20,000 in property taxes. I recently sold a three-family home on the west side, relocated to the east side. I've lived here since 2004, and I do love this city. My husband and I have settled in what should be our dream home. My husband is retired. He's a disabled veteran. He's on Social Security retirement. I work and our home is paid off. Yet, just to keep up with property taxes, we have to set aside nearly $900 a month. That's not for mortgage, not for insurance, not for water or sewer, which continues to rise at 9% a year, not for upkeep or repairs. That's just to pay for the tax bill on a home that we already own outright. If we fail to pay these taxes, even though our home is paid off, the city can ultimately take my home. That's a terrifying reality. And if I were to pass away, it's actually questionable whether my husband could shoulder the tax burden and remain in our long- term home. My husband and I have been having conversations. He is nearly 70 years old and disabled, and he may have to go back to work so we can establish a cushion against the rising taxes. That's not what retirement should look like, and it's not how we should be treating people who have spent their lives working and serving this country. The tax cap exists for a reason. It is a promise to residents that there is a limit to how much government will grow at their expense. Overriding the tax cap would be disastrous for homeowners and renters. I was an owner-occupied landlord for about 15 years in the city. I did see my rents going up in response to property taxes going up, and it is passed on to renters. Many families are already struggling, and I do feel people are going to be pushed out or priced out. I urge you, do not override the tax cap. Live within the means that Manchester residents are forced to live within. Find efficiencies. Set priorities and respect the limits that taxpayers are already hitting.

Brittany Ping, 199 Putnam Street: I was going to read Victoria's comments, but she said she's going to try to sneak back in if you call the roll. She had to go back to work. I live on the west side. It's the best side. I'm here to ask you guys to not override the tax cap. We had a budget tabled at the last meeting. There are more budgets that are being rumored to be presented. You know, we're listening to everybody talk about the things that we want for this city. Somebody said, this jug of orange juice was this amount and now it's this amount. And that's the reality of every single person, no matter what we believe, no matter what we're asking for, those are the decisions that our family has to make every day. You just don't buy orange juice, right? You buy Great Value. You buy the Minute Maid frozen, and you make it from concentrate. You make sacrifices. I didn't know those were bad things to instill in our children. I didn't know those were bad things to expect from our public officials. Those are things that I have to do every single day as a mom, as a wife, as a friend, as a business owner, as somebody who dedicates my time for non- profits throughout the city. Somebody that is trying to lift up people around me, shares my time, my treasure and my talents. And when the city says, I need more from you, Brittany, I need more from you, it's once again saying, if that's what you want, if you're going to override our taxes and you're going to, somebody said, I'm happy to pay more in rent, $50 a month. Let's pretend we get a 10 to 12% override after the assessments. We're looking at minimum about a $50 per month on an average rental in the City of Manchester, directly passed on to the next tenant. Now, maybe their lease is good through next fall. I'm about 75 days ahead in terms of leasing. So, we have people that are going to get the benefit. But then what does that tax increase look like next year? What are they going to do to us next year? Because it's never enough. So, to say it went from $5 to $11, let's figure out how the heck to make some cuts and afford that $5.

Jessica Spillers, 73 Jobin Drive: I'm here to support the community first budget. It's not the budget that I would have liked to see, but it is a good compromise. I've heard a lot of people here suggest that if you don't like what's happening in the public schools, send your kids somewhere else. Spend $15,000 and send them to Trinity. Where am I going to get $15,000 to send my kid to Trinity? I should buy concentrated orange juice? I already do. It is not easy in this economy for anyone, I get that, but there are 116,000 of us in this city, and if we all contribute a little bit, we can benefit a lot because the majority of people, just like me, send their kids to the public schools, and they deserve a good education just as much as those kids who go to Trinity, just as much as the kids who go to Saint Anthony's. And it frustrates me to hear people say that they are trying to live out their golden years, the best years, but they are somehow struggling. I understand that. I don't want to dismiss that, but it dismisses my reality as well. I'm in my late 30s. This should be a time when I'm at the peak and I am paying $4,000 a month for childcare for my three children. And if I say that I am willing to pay $50 more so that my kid can have a good education, so that their teacher can have supplies provided to them and they don't have to pay for it out of pocket, I think we can all figure that out. I am willing to sacrifice my peak so that my kids can have theirs, because at this point, that's what it's going to take. I hope that you will all keep that in mind. As you decide and you discuss this budget tonight, figure out what it is that we can do as a city because we can afford to do more. We have 116,000 people living here. And when we all come together as a community, we can be exceptional.

Melina Marescia, 181 Wilson Street: I'm here tonight to speak about my concerns regarding the proposed budget cuts and what they could mean for the children who rely on school transportation. My house is currently a bus stop for students attending Hillside Middle School and from where my house is located, the walk to the school is a long one. However, my concern goes beyond distance. It's about safety. Most, if not all of you, have children, grandchildren, nieces, nephews, or other young people in your lives. Would you feel comfortable knowing your middle schooler had to walk nearly two miles to and from school every single day? Would you worry about their safety? The issue doesn't only affect middle school students. It affects all children of all ages. Some parents do not have access to a car. Some leave for work before their children leaves for school. What happens when a third grader has to walk home alone and gets lost? What happens if another child is injured by a reckless driver while walking to or from school? In addition, did you know an estimated 38% of children who walk to school go missing? About 15% of those children are abducted by someone they know. So, I ask again, how would you feel as parents, teachers, neighbors, and community members? We trust our elected officials to make decisions that keep our children safe. Transportation is not a luxury. It's a necessity for families. When we talk about cutting bus routes, we're talking about placing additional risks and burdens on children and families throughout our community. I ask you to consider the real impact these budget decisions will have on our students. How would you feel if your child had to walk every single day alone? I urge you to protect our children's safety and preserve the transportation services they depend on.

Ken Harver: I'm going to speak loudly because I'm an old person. I know there's a lot of other old people in the room. As a sufferer of ADHD, and anybody who is familiar with it, you can understand the struggle I'm having trying to keep on one subject without these 20 squirrels running through my head at the same time. I'm going to avoid being political and I'm going to deal with factual logic. The school budget and the city budget, if I'm correct, are both about 80% fixed wages, benefits, maintenance costs, supply costs, things like that. I spent 20 years on the budget committee of a large adjoining town, and I learned that there are very few discretionary decisions that you can make. I checked this afternoon and I found that the CPI, while it sounds good, is an average. And the way averages work is you have outliers on both sides. And the issues that might be of interest and importance to the school district would be the cost of fuel and operation. I think your CPI is set at 3%. The cost of heating oil is up 75%. Your CPI is 3%. The cost of electricity is 12 to 17%. That's not political. That's facts. As much as you may want to, what control you have over this budget is absolutely minimal. I think it's important for people to understand that government is not a corporation. It's not run like a business. What government is, is a service industry. And as a service industry, it is heavily reliant on human beings, teachers, police, fire, DPW, janitors, all sorts of maintenance. That's fixed. That's not going anywhere. So, for people to tell me or say out loud, why don't you run it more like a business? I didn't get a chance to look at the school budget before I came here. If you look at the school budget or the city budget, you will find that they're tight. They're about as tight as you can possibly be. My experience in Londonderry, it is so frustrating dealing with people who just don't understand the reality of the situation. You cannot cut costs and you cannot control overruns when fixed costs are going up, triple the size of the rate of inflation.

Rob Chebook, Ward 4: I think it's funny that everyone's saying a tax cut. There's no tax cut. The budgets that are being proposed, we have a tax cap which the citizens of Manchester voted for. So, we're not cutting taxes. You're just raising them by what the tax cap was. I've lived here in my house 26 years, lived in Manchester over 30. I don't think I've ever seen a tax cut. If I'm wrong, someone let me know. There's never been a tax cut in Manchester. So, we have to stop playing games with words here. With the school, everyone's saying that we want to take money away from schools. No, no one's taking money away from schools. But we're consistently losing enrollment every year. We're down about 2,000 kids in the last ten years. So, at some point they should be able to balance their budget because they're losing kids every year. And it's funny because I saw an ad today, Manchester School District, they're complaining about vans that they have to bring food from the commissary to the schools. They weren't complaining because the vans were run down or they don't have them. They're complaining because they're plain white. So, they're holding a competition and it's great, they got the kids involved. They didn't hire some consulting firm and pay them millions of dollars to come up with a design. I think there's eight designs that they want people to vote on. Then they can have the vans wrapped in a school district that's saying they got to cut money from football or transportation or music, but they're going to spend money to wrap vans because they don't like that they're white. That's like a slap to the face of the taxpayers. Seriously, that's what we're looking for. We're looking for just good spending. That's what we're looking for. We just don't want you wasting our money.

Laura Burns, Ward 4: I'm a ward four resident for over 30 years. I am not right wing, I'm not left wing, because my wings are broken. I'm here to implore you to take the time needed to look at budget options that don't override our tax cap. Otherwise, why set a cap? Mayor, I voted for you solely because of your promises that you had made. Now they don't seem to mean too much, which has made me realize I can no longer trust you. I understand it's not an easy job and a hard decision to be made. But you took the job and you got the job by making promises to people like myself. I feel I was lied to. Please, board and mayor, work hard to find ways to keep within your spending limits. Skate park? No. Hanover Street redo? Really? Really, redo Hanover Street? It's beautiful. Engagement center? No. New school? No. Oh, the poor kids don't have windows. Really? Eyes should be all up front. Ears should be open to learning. The heck with what's outside. Maybe the test scores would go up. Line by line, item by item, get out your big red pen and keep your word and cut spending. Get a grip on the school board that is out of control in producing poor results. What happened to the local meetings with aldermen, police departments and the mayor? I don't see those happening anymore. Why are people allowed to be intoxicated in public? The people that choose to urinate in business doorways, pass out, or fentanyl freeze on our sidewalks that are also falling apart, they are all allowed to defecate and use drugs in our parks, our cemeteries. Why are they not arrested? I bet if they were arrested, I bet if arrests start to happen and they were not allowed to use their self-medication for an overnight in the clinker, they would stop parading around our beautiful city. Whom of you up here in front of all of us in this city, are willing to make the hard choices, to stop and cut and stop spending? I went to the library Saturday and I parked next to a sign that said no tents. And when I opened the car door, there were three tents at my feet. Why waste money on a sign if you're not going to enforce it? Just like children understand that their punishments are never really going to happen, they can rule the roost. There are no ramifications for their behavior. I feel this is the way our beautiful city is being run. Please look at this budget carefully, cut line by line, and stop wasting the city's money in foolish ways. The bike lanes? Nobody uses them. But we paid to have those paved. Nobody is using them. I've never seen a bike in the bike lane.

Mark Mackenzie, 319 West Erie Street: I am the Democratic representative from five wards in the City of Manchester. I can tell you what's going on here is the result of what happened up there. So, make no mistake about that. There is a consequence for what has happened over the last couple of years in Concord, but I'm not here to talk about that. I want to say how good it is to be with people who are engaged in the community, whether you're on one side or the other, you're here and you're fighting for what you believe in.
