I raised my children in this city, and it's a great place to live. I think we're all struggling with how we get to the place we need to be. The thing I wanted to mention today is the issue of the roads in this city. Over 50% of the roads in this city are either fair or poor. We have reports that have been done. We know what the issue is. We know it needs to be done within the City of Manchester. And if we don't do it, the only thing that we are going to end up with is more costly repairs to the roads than actually repairing the roads. You can't ignore the request that has been put in for $12 million to start bringing these roads back up to place. If you don't do that, then you will end up with a bill that is much higher, and you're going to end up with a whole group of people who are upset when they start bouncing around this city and potholes are all over the place. The people in the highway department are doing the very best they can, but they can't do it without the resources that are necessary. And make no mistake, if we don't move on this, if we don't do something, if we don't increase that budget, then you're going to end up in a position of having to spend a whole lot more money.

Sara Shannon-Yost, 435 Westwood Drive: I wrote a speech, but I figured we'll just go rogue. I'm not from Manchester originally. I moved here ten years ago from western Pennsylvania. Our school district is roughly the same size. But a few years ago, we had to choose to close schools. We had to find buildings that we could absorb to turn into schools that we could use so that we didn't have to spend millions and millions of dollars, that we didn't have to make a school much like how the charter schools do. I heard a lot of people talk about our school district and I have two sons. One is in the seventh grade at the Founders Academy. The other one is at Highland Goffs Falls School. My little guy at Highland has an IEP. He is autistic. The reason I didn't send my older one to Southside is because the last time I spoke here was to stop the fifth grade from being moved. The reason we're building additions onto schools now for God knows how much money is to facilitate those children. I chose not to send him there, because it would have been the second year that that fifth grade was. In the first year, there were marijuana vape pens being taken out of the fifth graders, there was a boys fight club in the bathroom, and that was not a safe place for my child. Now I was told, and I drank the Kool-Aid that your kids are safe when they go to school. Well, I didn't feel safe sending my child to that school. Sorry, but I wasn't. I am now in a predicament where I have to choose where to send my little guy. And unfortunately, I was told by the school district that we're not sure if we can have services sent to his charter school, because we may not have the funding for that. As a mother, I have to make that decision to send my child into a school that I was promised, and all these other parents were promised, when you guys sent the fifth grade into these middle schools, that they were going to be in a wing by themselves. That's not true. I implore all of you to go take a little visit, because there's seventh graders walking with fifth graders and the seventh graders that are in the little pods outside, some of them are going to be in the pods, but some of them are going to be by the fifth graders. That doesn't make them feel well. Also, I looked up the tax cap and I looked up why did you guys make a tax cap. Why are we sitting here even talking about it? Why did you make it in the first place if you're not going to stand by it? My house is worth $550,000. You know how much money that's going to be? I can't take my kids on vacation this year because we're living paycheck to paycheck. I'm sure all of you are as well. And I think that everyone in this city is as well. I don't know what you guys are going to do, but I think somebody said $50, it's not going to be $50 for me. And most people that own a house, it's not $50. So, I can shop at Aldi's all day long, but when I'm told that my special education child may not have services because I don't feel safe, there's a problem with our district.

Richard Girard, 283 Orange Street: It's time to bring some honesty into the budget discussions, which thus far have been fundamentally dishonest. The budget floated by Aldermen Terrio, Vincent, and Thomas, uses the same deceptive tactic deployed in the Democratic budget by comparing their proposed tax rate, which is based on a much larger tax rate to the current one, which is based on a substantially smaller tax base. They're misleading the people about the impact of the nearly $17.7 million tax increase their budget contains. When the denominators are made the same, which is basic elementary math needed to compare two numbers, one discovers that the 22.8% tax rate decrease shown on their budget sheet doesn't exist. It's a 10.14% tax increase, and while that's not much better than the proposed 11.8% increase in the Democrats’ budget, I have a question for Aldermen Terrio, Vincent, and Thomas. Can you, with straight faces, tell the same voters you promised you wouldn't override the tax cap, that there's an emergency that requires you to do just that and hand them a double digit tax hike that you tried to hide in a revaluation? I expected that from the Democrats, but not from you. In 1988, this city's tax base was $4.6 billion. When I took over as the mayor's budget director in 1995, it was $3.6 billion. We lost over 22% of the tax base. Not only that, we had millions in uncollected property taxes from cash strapped taxpayers. Elm Street and the millyard were practically abandoned. And the overlay account, that might as well have been a Pez dispenser. Somehow, though, we figured out ways to meet the needs of the city and make some of the very big changes that the first lady who spoke mentioned without layoffs, without disabling the everyday services this city relies on. And the tax hikes over those years didn't come anywhere near close to what's on the table now. Were there changes to how things got done? You bet. And here's the truth about government: it's a beast. Feed it continually and it will grow out of control just like it is now. Starve it and it will change. It's time to put the beast on a diet. Everything you're struggling with budgetarily, by the way, is of your own making. A big part of the non-tax city revenues the city lost is because you allowed the schools to use emergency reserves as one-time revenues for the specific purpose of avoiding spending cuts required by the tax cap. Also, last year, you padded spending with millions in one-time revenues from the phase one permit fees that were paid to the Planning Department. I don't know what happened at DPW, but their revenues cratered. You created this revenue hole. The board voted to approve budgets that added $4.7 million to the general fund by transferring dozens of positions created with one-time Covid grant funds to the operating budget, and greenlighting the massive increase in pay and benefits that came from recent compensation studies. This was on top of the $11 million in raises for teachers and other school employees in year one of their contract alongside a $20 million increase in annual spending for the ridiculously unnecessary phase one facilities plan. Either the mayor's budget or the Sapienza-Kantor budget will work for the city, and based on my personal experience in much harder budget times, I say that with complete confidence. Whatever you do tonight, I pray for this city's sake it's not a tax cap override. Double digit tax increases aren't good for anybody, especially perhaps for you Republicans that vote for them or fail to veto them.

Grisselle Glenn, Manchester: I'm off subject again, but equally as important nonetheless. I'm not going to repeat myself. I'm going to give some facts today, sourced facts. And then I'm going to tell you exactly what I expect you to do about them. Chief Marr and the mayor, listen carefully. After Nickenley Turenne was killed on December 6 th , Baliko, Chan and Lambert were placed on administrative leave. Chan was back on patrol in nine days. Baliko, 18 days. Lambert, 34 days. The AG investigation is still open. No findings, no determination. No footage released. When reporters asked the New Hampshire

Department of Justice why those officers were back on the street, Michael Garrity, the director of communications for the New Hampshire DOJ, said in writing, published in the Manchester Ink Link on April 23rd, returning an officer to duty is a decision made by their specific department. It is not a New Hampshire DOJ determination and does not mean that the investigation is complete or that the force was ruled justified. Not the DOJ's decision. Not the AG's decision. Yours. Manchester PD Public Information Officer Heather Hamel confirmed it in writing to the same outlet. The officers were approved to return after an administrative review completed by the department. She said they all returned. We followed our policy. Your policy, your review, your approval, Chief Marr. Now let's talk about consistency. On May 6th, Officer Ketchum stomped on the back of a handcuffed man on video. He was on administrative leave the next day. The Public Integrity Unit, a division of the New Hampshire Attorney General's Criminal Justice Bureau, was called in. A second officer in that same video punched the same handcuffed man in the legs and in his hands. And that officer is not on leave. Same video, same department, same chief. Three officers killed a man back on the street, 9, 18, and 34 days. One officer stomps a handcuffed man, leaves the next day. The second officer punches the same handcuffed man in the same video and nothing is done. So, Chief Marr, you make these decisions, not the AG, you do. And mayor, I need to address you directly. After I was removed from this room last time, you stood at that podium and said, you have full faith and confidence in Chief Marr and the men and women of the department, and that they do an extraordinary, difficult job. I want to be clear about something. These officers applied for this job. They were hired. They are paid by the city by taxpayer money, including mine. Difficulty is not a shield for accountability. Every person in this room who works a job is accountable for how they do it. And I would also note that it is very easy to have full faith and confidence in the department when you are not the one on the receiving end of the decisions. When you don't live in the neighborhoods they patrol, when you don't look like the people that they stop, chase, and shoot. That kind of trust is a luxury. The Turenne family does not have that luxury. This community does not have that luxury. The city charter places administrative authority in the city in your hands. The chief answers to you, which means every one of these decisions has your name on it, too. Here's what I'm demanding. Remove Baliko, Chan, and Lambert from active patrol pending the outcome of this investigation. Release the body camera footage to Nickenley’s family now and explain publicly on the record why your policy treated a stomp differently than a killing. You have always had the authority to act. The question is whether you have the integrity to use it.

Kathleen Paquette: I'm a New Hampshire state representative representing Manchester ward five. I'm here tonight to respectfully ask this board to pass a responsible, tax compliant budget. I serve on the Criminal Justice and Public Safety Committee, and I fully support funding the police contract. But the police contract should not be used to justify an entire budget that asks struggling taxpayers for even more. The proposal from two weeks ago included many other areas where spending could have been responsibly trimmed. I frequently receive calls from constituents who struggle because their taxes are already too high. People are scared. They're looking at rising costs of groceries, utilities, insurance, rent, mortgages and property taxes, and wondering how much longer they can sustain it. I'm sure many of you have heard the same concerns from your constituents. We are already facing a serious affordable housing crisis. Raising real estate taxes will only make that worse. Those costs do not stop with property owners. They get passed along in rents, and the people least able to absorb that extra cost are often hit the hardest. The tax cap exists for a reason. It's a protection voters put in place because they wanted accountability, discipline, and limits on how much more the government can ask from them. Manchester residents are desperately asking their leaders for relief, and a proposed budget ignores these pleas by shifting the burden of a bloated budget onto taxpayers who are already struggling to keep up. Several members of this board have spoken clearly in the past about protecting taxpayers. Alderman Trisciani commented in Manchester Ink link, I will respect the tax cap. Alderman Dan Goonan said as alderman, I will respect the tax cap and work tirelessly to keep taxes low, Alderman Terrio has said I support the tax cap because it's important to keep real estate taxes under control. I also have quotes from Alderman Thomas, Alderman Vincent, and even Mayor Ruais, that says they will protect the tax cap, use grants, efficiency surpluses. Dana Dexter, Dan O'Neil, words matter. Manchester heard them. Voters relied on them. Tonight, Manchester residents are asking this board to honor them. We can support public safety. We can support our schools and essential services. But we also have to support the people who pay the bills. Mayor Ruais said on WMUR at the end of every budget line is a family that has to pay for it. Tonight, I ask you to remember those families. Respect the tax cap. Hannah Kesselring, Ward 12: I'm 12 years old and I live in Manchester ward 12. Thank you for giving me the chance to speak tonight. I know I'm younger than most people who speak here, but the decisions you make today will affect my future and the future of other kids growing up in Manchester. Over the last few years, I've spent time sitting in BMA meetings and learning about city budgets and bonding. I've learned that when a city issues bonds, it's borrowing money that has to be paid back later with interest. That means decisions made today can create costs for taxpayers in the future. As someone growing up in Manchester, that matters to me. One day I hope to buy a home, have a family and build my life here. But I worry that if spending keeps growing, borrowing keeps increasing, and taxes continue to rise, it may be harder for young people like me to stay in the city we love. Everything already costs more than it used to. Housing is expensive. Groceries are expensive. Energy bills are expensive. Families are doing their best to keep up. If taxes continue rising because of increased spending and borrowing, my generation will eventually be the ones helping carry that burden. I understand that the city has important responsibilities. We need safe roads, public safety, and services people rely on every day. I also believe that just because the city can borrow money doesn't always mean it should. Borrowing now means paying more later. I think the city should focus on priorities, spend taxpayer dollars carefully, and try not to place unnecessary debt on future generations whenever possible. I'm wearing an American flag pin on my blazer. The reason we have the freedom of our flag is because men went to war to get it. There was the Boston Massacre, the Boston Tea Party, and, of course, the Revolutionary War. I think the city should focus on priorities. The choices you make tonight won't only affect people living here today, they will affect kids like me, who will one day inherit the responsibility of paying for them. Please keep Manchester affordable, keep taxes under control, and don't break the tax cap.

Steve Kesselring, Ward 12: I don't really normally follow my daughter, but this is a different one for me. I serve as a state representative for ward 12. I live on Hackett Hill Road in Manchester. So, before this meeting, I asked a couple constituents that have been emailing me over the last few days, and they said a couple of things that they've been feeling the pressure from, not just the property taxes over the last few years. They felt the pressure on the increased water and sewer that's coming, and they're scared about what's going to come from that. They said that the cost of energy, one person mentioned it was over 35% this year, that she had to increase the rent because one of them is a renter, has gone up 10% year over year, every single year. Insurance costs, car insurance. Every single thing is going up. I understand that there's costs that have to go up with every single budget. I see that at the state level, I see all the things that have to come to us. So, what I'm saying tonight, and I want to say this very bluntly, think about those people, think about all of those things that have to be paid for and what your increase would look like for those people. I want to end with two things. One, we have a lot of things to be proud of here in Manchester. We are ranked number one in a lot of categories, but do we want to be ranked number one in the highest taxes in the state? I think you need to think about that tonight when you talk about the budget, and I want to end with this. I'm about to not make any friends at DPW, but download the app SeeClickFix and everybody take pictures of those potholes because I do it in ward 12. And if you drive around, ward 12 has a lot of potholes that are all filled in and within 24 to 48 hours, they normally fill them in. So, take some pictures on SeeClickFix.

Daniel Mowery, Ward 6: You all know who I am. I live in ward six. I'm very popular with this board and with the city of Manchester. Because we're sick and tired of wasteful spending. Another thing is when the member at large for the school board, it's amazing how she says that these kids going to parochial school are being bussed by the city of Manchester. Those residents pay taxes, so they deserve a bus ride to the parochial school, charter school, wherever they go, because they're paying for a better education doesn't mean they should have to pay for their own transportation. So therefore, I ask the Board of Alderman and mayor, do not overspend the tax cap. Your constituents have plastered you over social media. Tell the truth. Do what you promise. Rick Soule, Ward 1: Thank you all for your service. Please don't override the tax cap. The skateboard park is nothing if you can't afford a skateboard. A swimming pool is no good if you can't afford swimming lessons. Please don't override the tax cap.

Pat Long, Ward 3: Last week I attended this Football Scholar Athlete Award. There were 38 recipients. I was proud that one of them was Jacob Eli Henry from Manchester West. The only person from Manchester West. Very proud of him. He's distinguished himself in the classroom and on the field of play. That's something that I've heard people talk about. You can hear from me on what I think should happen on your budget. You hear from individuals what should happen on their budget. That is your decision. Your decision; only your decision. You do the due diligence. Every budget that I looked at, and there's three proposals I looked at, they all increased taxes. Hearing that people’s rents are going up 10% a month, I don't recall our budgets going up 10% a month. I'm dealing with elder women that have left their apartments because they went from $1,400 to $2,200 a month. They can't afford that. One of them is living on somebody's couch. That's what I'm dealing with. So, in my opinion, rents are market based. If I'm a landlord, I'll get what I'll get, whatever I can get. There are some landlords that don't do that. They try to stay within a reasonable fixed cost. And that, I appreciated. But there's way too little of that. Two weeks ago, I heard an increase would raise rents. We had a child speak two weeks ago. I'm hearing that the increase in taxes, people aren't coming here. People are coming here. There was a child that spoke two weeks ago. Their parents bought a home in Manchester from Auburn. Manchester offers them. That's why they moved to Manchester. That's what we have to keep up. I have thirty seconds. Thank you, Deputy Clerk, I waited to hear that thirty seconds. I should have heard it more when I was on the other side of this aisle.

Kathy Turgeon, Manchester: I will be 80 years old in 20 days. I am retired. I'm on a fixed income. However, I expect you and the board to come to an agreement that will see you supporting the Police Department, improving our roads and sidewalks, and making sure that teachers who go back to school this fall will have the supplies they need to teach our children. A gentleman spoke earlier saying that our schools do not send children to college who need a year of remediation. My daughter, a product of Manchester schools K through 12, went to college on a presidential scholarship. Her daughter, a product of Manchester public schools, valedictorian of Central High School, just completed her first year at Dartmouth with straight A's. Now, how can a child from a bad school system do that? It also not just teachers, it's parents. It's the whole community. And let's talk about losing students. That doesn't mean you're going to lose a principal, an assistant principal, an aide for the special ed kids that you have in class, an interpreter for the diverse population you have. One year, I had 33 first graders that I taught. The parents complained when they came to open house and had to sign their names on the board and wait for their turn to speak to me. I said, imagine then, how your first grader feels if they have to wait for 33 other kids. Let's have some common sense. Let's look forward, not backwards. Elaine Dallaire, 361 Hayward Street: I'm here about the ADA sign. It's an update. I have had several unwanted confrontations with angry YMCA members and others inside and outside of the facility. The officer wanted to know why the parking enforcement department was not going to the street and stopping people from parking beyond their time limits. Same answer. Officer wanted to know why the YMCA did not help me, and I told him they did not care about getting directly involved in lessening my hardships. As tensions rise, employees from the YMCA, only a few, are writing me out where there was no pattern to suggest any harsh treatment against me. Deb Roux, Ward 12: Before I begin, I just want to ask you to please stay underneath the tax cap. It's there for a reason. I want to say that I urge you to support and I want to thank Alderman Kantor and Sapienza for doing the work and making a budget that works for everybody. I appreciate it, and I'm holding this sign here because I'm trying to educate everybody on the founding of our country and the principles our country was founded on. And our founders believed in God, and they trusted God, and they followed God in all of their decisions. And I don't know if anyone saw that on May 17th in Washington, D.C., there was a 9.5 hour to rededicate America as one nation under God. And one thing our founders believed was that our inalienable rights come from God. And one of those important rights was the right to own property. When our founders first started this country, everybody was kind of going in the same building, planting and doing everything as one area. But then that wasn't working because people weren't pulling their weight. And so, they gave everybody their own property. And as soon as they had their own property, things started to prosper. And in trying to keep your own property these days with rising taxes, and what I'm trying to say is that when you have your own property, it's supposed to be your own property. You're not supposed to be taxed out of it and be able to take your property from you, because that's one of our rights that is so important for all of us in this day and age to have. And when you have to go and pay for something that you've already purchased over and over again, it's just not right. And our schools need to be held accountable. One of the things our founders also said was that they believe passing debt onto the next generation was a sin. And as Hannah nicely stated, that if we keep borrowing and having to pay, all that interest rate is going to cost the next generation more money. I'm urging you to hold the schools accountable. Make them increase the grades for our students and just be more fiscally responsible so that we don't, as taxpayers, have to keep paying more than necessary and eventually possibly losing our homes because of it. These biblical principles and what our founders created was what made America and our nation so prosperous, so generous, and so innovative. I ask you to keep that in mind as you go to vote tonight, that we are paying so much for something that we have the right to have.

Kathleen Carswell, Ward 4: I've lived in Manchester my 64 out of my 66 years of being here and I grew up here. I went through all the school systems. I went to Ash Street, Pearl Street, Hillside and Central, and I graduated. I didn't go off to school. I worked for my family's company, but I saw hardship. Why don't we take the little gravel pit next to the soup kitchen, build a ten story building there, put the engagement center on the first floor, have the homeless come there that want the help, and if they don't want the help, give them a bus ticket to where they came from. I'm tired of paying. I pay rent and I'm getting rented out basically. I can't afford to be where I am. I'm going to be homeless and that shouldn't be. I worked, I put in my time. I put in my hours. We can save money. Do that. Why can't we do that? I don't understand this. We spend millions of dollars on all these different buildings that you rehab that two years down the road, we got to turn around and find another building. That money we can put towards schools. We can put towards police departments, roads, we can put towards our needs we need in this city. I love the city. I don't want to have to go anywhere else. I can't afford to go anywhere else. I can't find a place to go. I'll be living in a tent in the park with people I don't want to live with. We got pedophiles like there's no tomorrow. Homeless in the city of Manchester. I don't know if there's a notice going out to these people, but every time I look on Facebook on these predatory groups that follow these people, we're getting more and more here. We're getting more and more homeless. I'm tired of picking up needles in my neighborhood. I shouldn't have to be going around and picking up needles so that the kids don't pick them up or touch them because you don't know what's in that stuff for these kids. And they shouldn't have to pay to play a sport in high school or any school. I was lucky enough I didn't have to pay. I played tennis and volleyball in high school. I had to walk all the way up to Webster Street from Central High School to play tennis. I played with my father's wooden tennis racket. I'm a proud citizen of Manchester, but it's getting to be to the point where it's not physically and financially supporting me or my friends, who are all elderly here. A lot more elderly than you think. And we're building these so-called affordable apartments. They're not affordable. They take up our paycheck before we can pay anything else. How are we supposed to live on that? We can't. We have to start thinking about resources here instead of spending foolishly.

Serena Mackay, Ward 4: I am a junior at the Founders Academy. It is a charter school here in Manchester. Same time last year, I remember my peers and I standing before this board writing the same speeches to advance student calls for better facilities that reflect the true potential of Manchester's students. First, I would like to thank those who have played a major role in the improvements that we have seen recently in Manchester schools. These changes would not have been possible without thoughtful leadership and the proper allocation of resources to our schools. But too often, budget discussions become centered on numbers and percentages, and we forget that behind every single dollar allocated or cut are real people, students, teachers, families, and community members whose lives are directly affected by these decisions. When these schools receive the support that they need, students are actually able to learn in environments that are safe, that are functional, and conducive to success. But when we don't take this into account, how are we supposed to build a Manchester that is livable? We don't want to hear it from parents who can afford to send their kids to private school. We cannot have a Manchester, a place where families have relied on and resided in for generations, become something that disregards the very backbone of its community. We urge this board and the people in this room to support the community first budget. Why? Because we believe in investing in the students, the families, and the public services and servants who make Manchester strong. Let's put community first.

Dylan Torres, 622 Lake Avenue: While I appreciate the proposed $2 million increase to school budgets, I really don't think it's a good idea to pull funds from other parts of our city, especially when there are complaints all over from lack of funding. I'm in support of the community first budget, even if it means a tax increase. Our roads are covered in potholes and while I was working as a flagger, I left the city from just about every prominent exit. And in many of them there were potholes that made me feel like I hit a curb. And I have no doubt it contributed to the wear on my car's suspension, not to mention the lack of flagging work in Manchester already on account of the roads almost never being repaired. Changing out my suspension is going to cost me thousands. Not even mentioning potential damage to ball bearings, rods, or my alignment, far more than any tax increase would impose. This is something that all drivers will have to deal with. Why is it that our city is one of the most prominent in the state, yet we have to compromise even further between the education of our students and acceptable road conditions? I'd feel a lot happier about where my taxes are going if I didn't have to wiggle my car through a minefield, or have to worry about the conditions of our schools and their facilities properly accommodating students. If we're going to be taxed anyways, I want it to at least properly fund the city.

Sue Corby, 2094 Elm Street: I am here to support the budget that was presented at the last meeting, May 19th. That's a compromise budget that doesn't fund the schools or the city departments as much as requested or as much as needed. But it does keep our wheels turning. It necessitates overriding the tax cap. Overriding the tax cap is not something anyone takes lightly, but I and many others believe it's necessary this time. Not every year, but this time. Yes, the tax cap is there for a reason, but also for a reason there's a provision for overriding it in certain situations, and I think we're there right now. Specifically, we need to fund the police so they can fill their roster and compete with surrounding towns to hire really good policemen who know how to work in an urban environment. We need to provide funding for repairing our streets, our sidewalks. We need to fund our schools, keep a decent teacher student ratio and provide opportunities for our arts, athletics and academics. These things keep kids in school and out of trouble. We need to keep employing community health workers because they provide important health information and services to people who might not otherwise get that information or those services. They are really crucial. We need to keep the West Side library open again. This is a compromise budget. It doesn't fully fund city departments or the schools. There is lots of talk about protecting the taxpayer. But who is the taxpayer? The taxpayer and the consumer of the city services that the taxes pay for are one and the same. It's us. We protect ourselves by limiting the taxes as we have, especially in the last two years. Maybe too much. Maybe it's causing us problems now. But that's one way we protect ourselves. We also protect ourselves by providing ourselves with services, and we need to keep us safe, healthy, and educated. We should be looking at this budget not in terms of a punitive negative tax, but in terms of contributions that we all need to make to pay for the services that we need.

Ken Tassey, Ward 6: I'm a former school board member in Manchester and the chairman of the Manchester Republican Committee. I'd like to address the budget and the tax cap debate, but I'd first like to express my concern over statements made by some of the aldermen. Two weeks ago, in the previous BMA meeting, 2 or 3 aldermen had made comments intended, in my opinion, to intimidate anyone who opposes their views, accusing those who don't think the way they do of being against our police force. That's dangerous rhetoric. It's insulting and it's a lie. Now, all the while, they are disregarding the substance that's been given tonight by many giving testimony here tonight about the hardships of being a retiree, living on a fixed income, and being taxed out of their homes and maybe taxed out of the city. There was a mention tonight also by one of the younger members giving testimony tonight about rent, and rent for a two-bedroom apartment five years ago was $1,200. Now it's over $2,000 and that is directly related to the cost of taxes by the people who own those buildings. So please, if discussion ensues tonight on this particular matter, I ask those people to please hold your tongue and be respectful to those who don't believe the same way you do about how to move the city forward. I'd also like to mention a school board member of high rank recently went on record in the Union Leader, stating that the time has come to give our school board full autonomous taxing authority. And that basically means that everyone in the city who owns a property would get two tax bills, one from the city and another one from the school district. That was developed, that was put together on the whim of tax and spend committee members. Be careful what you wish for because the pendulum swings both ways and we don't want to remove that system of checks and balances. Finally, on the tax cap, I'll ask you to humor me while I give just a quick personal analogy about what compromise is. My wife is about this much shorter than I am. When we walk together, she walks a little faster. I walk a little slower. And that's something that we agree on, that we own. But you don't own the taxpayers’ money. The tax cap itself is already a compromise. It's something that the city and the people of the city have already agreed on. It's a slow increase in taxes. Please vote to not exceed the tax cap.

Angel Brisson, Ward 8: My family are Manchester taxpayers, including my in-laws, who are seniors on fixed incomes. I'm here to implore the board to not override the tax cap. Instead, the responsible decision, the solution that respects taxpayer wallets, that respects our financial limitations, is to adopt either the mayor's budget or Alderman Sapienza and Alderman Kantor's budget. Some compromise there in those budgets, increase our taxes by just under 3%, around 3%, versus the unconscionable and untenable 12% tax increase wanted by the Democrats or the equally unacceptable 10% tax increase proposed in the Vincent-Thomas budget. Those unacceptable, 12% and 10% increases, will more than double our property taxes, bringing our taxes to almost triple what's allowed under the tax cap. I personally don't know anyone who has received a 10% or 12% raise this year. You have a fiscal responsibility to your constituents to uphold the tax cap. That's what we voted for. The tax cap exists to put reasonable limits on spending. Why have a tax cap if the board is just going to override it when it pleases, thereby betraying the public's trust? We taxpayers have to live within our personal budgets, making allocations, reallocations, sacrifices, changes, choices without a constant influx of new funds from someone else's household. And the city should manage its taxpayer funded budget as well. Again, the solution is to hold the tax cap by adopting a budget that does so.

Bob Fuller, Manchester School District: I'm a very long-time teacher at Memorial High School teaching social studies. I'm here tonight to give a simple message. Elections have consequences. I'll explain. A majority of this board has presented a budget that at least more than half agree to. The school board recently voted by a majority vote to not remove teachers. When I came in the next day, I ran into a lot of people who were very grateful that they had not lost their lifetime dream to then teach kids and for the school board, personally, professionally, I'm very grateful for the stand they took. A majority of you have expressed support for the schools and for other important city services like roads, police and fire. Because that's what a vibrant community needs to have. When I was born in the city over a half century ago, and seeing all the things that I've seen and what the school board did, and I could be wrong on this, I've never seen a stand like that. If you have a stand like that, you know that something really is going either right or wrong. Right or wrong is a pretty simple thing. Now, when it comes to this and you hear all the things about raising taxes and everything else, what's being talked about tonight is a revenue override. It's not taxes being raised. It's a permission to use excess revenue. And where that revenue come from, that came from a reevaluation of property. Now, where did all that money come from? A revaluation of property. You know where it comes from. People move here for schools. That's the number one reason why they come here. That's why they do the work they do. Because that's how you build a great community. That's how you get economic growth. You get it through the schools. That's where growth comes from. So, it's a pretty simple proposition that that money, which is the people's money, which was raised through a lawful reevaluation, of which again, in between, people have had a chance to actually have an election and elect people, because the last budget cycle, this room was different. Some of you were the same, some of you were different. But there's a lot of different people here because people wanted a change. They wanted support for schools, police, fire. Looking at one of the other budgets, you have a massive decrease in schools and roads. Now why are you going to do that? I mean, I've worked in the city now for almost 30 years. For a time here, when the roads were in really bad shape, my car would literally tell me I was in Manchester because there's potholes everywhere. It's the pothole tax. So, you either pay a little bit now or you pay a little bit later. So, as you're looking at this, yes, you have a very tough decision here. I get that. But remember, elections have consequences. I implore you to support the budget that a majority of you actually support.

Sue Hannon, Manchester Education Association: I am the president of the Manchester Education Association. Understanding that, hearing all the sides of this argument and debate tonight, I certainly understand the reticence of people who are looking at increases in their taxes and what they have to provide to the city. I think we need to remember that when we're talking about prices that are going up for gas and water and electricity and rent and so on, are other entities in the city having to deal with that as well? I can speak as far as what I know about the school district. We have to pay all those things. We don't get water and electricity for free. We're paying for buses that have hundred-gallon tanks. And imagine the insurance on a school bus full of children. People speaking tonight, in some cases, made the city sound like it was the worst place on earth to be. But I have to disagree. I don't live here, but I love coming to Manchester. Manchester is awesome. Manchester provides so much for the people who live here. So much activity, so much fun, so much excitement. But it also provides education. It also provides the things that we need in a city this size. Obviously, taxes are going to help you with being able to continue to provide those things. We may have some low scores in the Manchester school district. Absolutely, but those scores come from tests that make us act like we are testing 12,000 of the exact same students. They are not individualized. The education our teachers provide is individualized. It's very different. We have students who move on to amazing careers, students who attend Ivy League schools, students who earn full rides to schools. Please understand that the district the school district has lost 10 to 15 positions per year since I've been doing this due to attrition. The thing that is not talked about all that often, where we are losing staff, just as we're losing some students. And that's something you all need to talk about as far as attracting people to come here. We are losing staff on a continual basis. And please make no mistake, the school district itself did lose 2.5% last year. Taxes were cut by 2.5% in the district, so we need to make some adjustments here. But a budget that is funding what we need to do in this city is of utmost importance.

Ronald Rose, Ward 2: I'm the aquatics director of the Manchester, New Hampshire YMCA, and I am a selectman for ward two. Our YMCA has been a community partner for Manchester for well over 100 years. Our building nearby City Hall struggles to serve some members of our community because of a lack of parking spaces. Handicapped parking spaces on Stark Street are very limited, and the YMCA members who need them find them unable to use our facility. The YMCA wants to continue to serve our community, and we're asking that some handicapped parking spaces be added to Stark Street at the earliest convenience.

Ryan Drohan, Ward 7: It seems a large majority on this board hold a belief that taxpayers have deep pockets. And yes, that is true that taxpayers do have deep pockets. It is because they have a hole in their pockets. Taxpayers are struggling with inflation and food, gas, childcare, housing, health insurance and sewer rates in Manchester being raised by 19% every year from 2025 through 2028 and 15% in 2029, for a grand total of a 96% increase. Property taxes going up exponentially will affect renters and individuals on fixed incomes. The effect is they will become destitute and homeless. I support Aldermen Sapienza and Kantor’s budget passing tonight. It's an excellent balance for the city and the taxpayers. Don't break the tax cap.

Troy Micklon, 29 Ode Way: I'm here once again to urge the board to reject the budget proposal by Alderman Burkush and Trisciani, as well as the other tax cap busting budgets being presented tonight. The tax cap was adopted by Manchester voters for a reason. It exists to ensure that government spending grows at a sustainable pace and that taxpayers are protected from excessive increases year over year. Families across Manchester don't get to override their household budgets when expenses go up, they have to make difficult choices, prioritize needs over wants, and live within their means. The city government should be expected to do the same thing. Furthermore, these alternative budgets are being proposed with a lack of transparency and details. If taxpayers are being asked to pay more, we deserve a clear explanation of exactly where the money is going and why the board should be able to explain each line item increase and the reasons behind what's driving them. We should also be provided with a better understanding of what the genuine needs are versus discretionary wants. I also want to point out that later this evening, the board will receive an update by the updated financial projections from the Finance Director. Those projections will show an anticipated FY 26 general fund operating surplus of approximately $1.9 million. This is another increase in our surplus since the last meeting, showing that the city's financial position is in better shape than some others would have us believe. This board also has two other budgets to consider. The budget proposed by you, Mr. Mayor, and the one by Aldermen Kantor and Sapienza. These are both under the tax cap and help keep Manchester on the right path. And I urge the board to consider them. And finally, Mr. Mayor, I want to address one more thing. The Union Leader recently referenced a member of this board, where he suggested that citizens who come here and speak against the tax cap are somehow threatening. Respectfully, the only real threat is that we'll remember at the next election who voted to override the tax cap.

Glenn Ouellette, Ward 3: As important as these discussions are, as you notice that it is 9:30 p.m., my curfew is at 9 p.m. I hope they let me in tonight. I will say that my rent last September went up $845. You tell me if 48.9% increase in rent is an affordable rent. It is not. I will also tell you that so far this year, since January, I have expended $7,000 out of my pocket for medical attention besides insurance. So yes, costs go up. The good news is I'm getting back on my feet. So, you have to spend sometimes to make things go. But I don't like waste. And we have a past in this city where we wait till things are so broken up that we're going to tear them down and start back from scratch. That's what we've been doing in the past with our schools. Do you know how many times we've changed our administration of the school in the last 20 years? Too many times. $7.5 million in the last ten years. We're not thinking. But this is what's important. We now have a budget in the school system that is $400,000 short for occupying and educating our special ed. Shame on us. You have too many administrators in the school system; assistant superintendents, it is just too many. We need to find ways to cut the budget and it shouldn't be on the students. The other thing I say about education is public education is based on equality for every student in this city, and to have sports or other activities like music, to only go to kids whose parents can afford to pay, is not a public education, and that is unconstitutional and it should not be tolerated. So, make sure that when you do your budget today that those holes are filled in. There are ways to cut the budget. The last thing I will say is that our police department, if you were to hire those police officers that are now not in office, you wouldn't have to pay a million and a half or more per year in time and a half. That is a waste of money. Our money is better put in having the manpower, getting their regular wages.

Roger Bleau, Ward 1: First of all, I feel sorry for all of you politicians. You're taking so much crap tonight. I feel really bad for you. This is going to be tough. But first of all, I just want to say I support your budget. I think that's reasonable and I think it's necessary. I'm all for the kids. That's the first thing I always think of is the school system. That's what I care about the most because I care about the kids the most. I remember years ago they had the GI Bill when soldiers came back from World War Two, they invested in the newly released soldiers, and we boomed after that. So, education is the most important thing, I think, of taxes as revenue, not as a burden. I really do. I think it's necessary to keep that in mind. What we're doing is we're putting revenue for things we think are important. And also, I think swill falls downhill. Our federal government under this administration has cut money for education, among other things. Our state government has violated the New Hampshire Constitution by not providing enough funds for our city. We're only getting a little over $4,000 per kid. And the Constitution said we should get at least $7,000. Unbelievable. So, we're not doing that. I saw a thing once, a while ago, and they said, in a real good society, you don't need charity because the government should figure out a way to take care of everybody. It means increased taxes, but it's worth it. The other thing I want to talk about is Governor Ayotte is always talking about don't Mass up. Do you know if you compare Massachusetts in every department, they are doing better than us because they're willing to pay for their kids, their teachers average $92,000 a year, because that's a priority for them? I think it's good if we work on that. The other thing is we have inflation. It's unbelievable. The current president broke his promise about not going to war. How much money are we spending on that? The current president promised that he'd reduce prices on day one. So, the school budget, the police, everybody is under tremendous pressure because that administration caused inflation. So, if we don't raise the tax to just cover the increases in cost, then we're just definitely going backwards. And my honest opinion, inflation is not 3%. It's at least 10%. The amount of money I spend on gas and heating oil and food, it's unbelievable. I recommend you vote for June Trisciani’s thing. I think it's important and I think it's good for the kids and it's good for the city.

Kay Emery, Ward 3: While I understand and can appreciate the intention of trying to remain under the tax cap, I find the originally proposed budget unsustainable and antithetical to the intention of keeping Manchester running as is, let alone improving it for current and future residents. As an active young resident who frequently runs and bikes around the city, in fact, I biked here tonight, I was particularly shocked by the lack of funding for our Department of Public Works and equally disheartened to see our education department so under-supported. As I contemplate starting my own family in the next couple of years, it pains me to imagine that I may have to leave the city and my community here to be able to provide my child with a strong education. I also find the decision to withdraw from the Southern New Hampshire Planning Commission to be a clear mistake, as the Commission has been critical to several improvements in the city, including securing funds for improvements in numbers that make the cost of their annual fee a strong investment. I fear that the withdrawal from the Southern New Hampshire Planning Commission will cripple Manchester's ability to competitively apply for and receive funds from the federal government programs such as the Brownfields

Redevelopment Program that must be utilized if we truly wish to improve the city while attempting to be creative about how we are funding these improvements. Looking at the mayor's originally proposed budget, I feel a sense of dread that I might need to begin planning for a future somewhere else. I hope that the leadership in this room understands that safer sidewalks and streets, strong, well-funded public education, and planning for increased resilience in this city is a non-negotiable for someone looking to start a family and put down roots here.

Elyza Agosta, Ward 2: I'm here to speak today to speak in favor of the compromise budget and overriding the tax cap. I'm a young person in Manchester who owns a home and works here. I'd like to live here for many more years as I found a strong and welcoming community. I'd like to send my kids to the Manchester schools, walk downtown on sidewalks, and be able to drive or bike without worrying about potholes. To be able to have a future with those basic needs met, we need to properly fund our city government. It's that simple. I strongly empathize with those on a fixed budget. This is the main issue with relying so heavily on property tax. Property tax is a flat tax across the board. Unlike a tax with brackets, we cannot separate high earners from those on fixed incomes. This means that as the New Hampshire population grows older, on average, we are funding our city less and less while needing to provide more and more. This is unsustainable. If exemptions need to be made for those on fixed incomes or a different taxation system needs to be put in place, I would support that. However, that is not the choice we have in front of us today. We need to fund our city government this year. Everyone knows that prevention is the key. If we don't come up with the necessary maintenance, we will end up with future issues that are much harder to fix. I challenge anyone who thinks we can trim the fat and get rid of excess waste to actually sit down with a city staff member and see what they do on a day-to-day basis. I've seen it being on the Planning Board, MTA board, and the Southern New Hampshire Planning Commission Board. I've never seen people do so much with so little resources. I work at a private company and I've seen waste and inefficiencies. The city staff works to find creative ways to offer necessary services while being constantly underfunded year after year. Mayor and Aldermen, by underfunding our city year after year, you are holding Manchester's future and my future hostage. Please consider voting for the compromise budget and overriding the tax cap. Jess Harkness, Ward 3: I'm here tonight to express my concerns relating to the originally proposed budget. It's disheartening to see proposed reductions in many crucial public service departments. A community that does not reliably invest in the next generation and their educators will not have a bright future. Nearly everyone here has cheered for the students who have spoken tonight. We love to hear from passionate and intelligent young people. But evidently many of those cheering will still choose to advocate for policies that undermine their futures and undermine the livelihoods of their educators. The proposed budget devalues the immediate everyday needs of our communities, like having well- maintained roads, safe sidewalks, strong local transportation systems, and a well- supported public education system. These are not luxuries that people are asking for. These are basic needs for a safe and functioning community with rising fuel costs. Many people, myself included, are traveling more by foot, by bus, and by bike. It is your duty as public servants to see that the infrastructure of our communities can meet those demands. I strongly urge you to vote in support of the proposed compromised budget, which would restore funding to some of the aforementioned community services. I'd like to add that personally, I use the bike lanes nearly every day. In fact, I used them to get to this meeting tonight.

Leslie Want, Ward 4: My husband and I moved here in 1991 and I have lived here for the last 35 years. We have loved living and raising our two children here and sending them K through 12 to the Manchester School District. Manchester is a big, beautiful tapestry, diverse of cultures, arts, arts venues, beautiful parks, libraries and a humming downtown. And perhaps most importantly, vibrant public schools that serve our city's little ones and teens, helping them to enter college, the trades, and or military service. That beautiful tapestry called Manchester, needs funds to support every aspect, to continue to be a city that people are drawn to. By failing to fund the things that make our community strong, you pull the threads of this community tapestry and you cause it to be less beautiful, less able to serve the people of our community. I ask you to think about Manchester 10 to 20 years from now. What do you want it to be? What do you want your legacy to be? Do you want the beautiful tapestry of Manchester to continue, or will you let the city tapestry become shabby and worn through lack of investment? I ask you to please support the budget.

Nick Want, Ward 4: So, it's sort of interesting sitting here listening to the comments. And I've spoken before and I'll be reiterating a couple of those. So, the issue that we have with the tax cap is that we're not abiding by the tax cap. We have people back here with signs being held up to defend the tax cap. The tax cap has multiple purposes. One of them and one of the big ones is to prevent overspending by the government and by our officials. Absolutely. Totally agree. We don't want people just to raise our taxes to a large amount of money based on whims. So, the ability to limit the spending is a good thing. However, it also provides a guide. It is based on an index related and attached to inflation. So, it is a guide for those people who don't understand budgets as well as to what they should in fact spend their money on. And so, this mayor woefully underfunded the last two tax budgets that we've had. So, we have people here to defend the tax cap. I agree; defend the tax cap. But if the tax cap is telling you that you should be spending 4.5% as we should have done last year, but instead we spent 2.4%, we failed. You failed. You let your leadership fail us. This is why we’ re in the predicament we're in today. Your last two budgets were supported by members of this Board of Alderman. A number of them are not here anymore. So, when people talk about votes mattering, votes do matter because those people aren't here. Who supported you? You have the option to appropriately fund our city. If we had not underfunded the last two budgets, we would be sitting here today talking about where will we come up with a $1 million difference. Instead, the main difference that we have in our underfunded budget is because you led us down this path. You have the option, Mr. Mayor, to understand and realize what we have done here and to fix it. You have a new board that's been replaced by some of the people who supported you before, because people realize this is not the path that Manchester wants to go down. Schools are important, but also our roads’ situation, our DPW, the fact that you underfunded our DPW by $6 million last year, and most of the people who wish to defend the tax cap also mention we have terrible roads. Yes, we have terrible roads because you underfunded it by $6 million. And so, this year we need to compensate and adjust and make up for the revenue that you failed to provide to this city to support it. The tax cap also supports not just the taxpayers, but it supports the city. It provides the city that we all want to live in. You need to fix this, Mr. Mayor. You made this mess. You have the option to lead the solution.

Karolyn Gomes, Ward 6: Crissy and I have talked numerous times, and I do support her budget. First of all, I want to say that I do support the Manchester Police Department and Fire Department. I say thank you even in stores when I see them. The roads are horrible. I drive on them every day. And we do pay $5 on our car registration to fix and repair the roads. If you want to talk about the budget, the teachers and administrators pay is outrageous. While sitting here, I googled what the superintendent makes. She makes $203,359. Do you make that, mayor? I don't think so. Do I make that? I don't think so. And sure, maybe she works the whole year. But the teachers, if you look at their pay, it could go anywhere from $50,000 to $100,000 a year. But they're not working a year. So, I think we really should look at the bottom line. The schools have touch screen TVs that are not used. I know this for a fact because I had two kids in the school district, and I still have one that's still in the school district. 90% of the teachers don't teach. They give out packets and say, go do your assignments. I know this for sure because one of my kids has a teacher that gives out packets every day, 20 pages long, doesn't teach. The school buses are always late. I get texts every single morning. Thank God I don't need a school bus right now. The scores that everybody says Manchester is so low, they're false. I know that because when my kids were in elementary and even in middle school, they just want to get through it. They pick any old answer without even reading it. Teachers are not doing their job. I spend a lot of time on i-Ready with my kids. Not worth it. Good old-fashioned teaching should be there. I really think we should look for people that can run a budget like moms. We go to the store. I think what Victoria Sullivan said a few weeks ago, live within our means. Yes, I support Crissy’s budget and we really need to look at it. If the people want their schools and everything else and support the override, let them donate the money to invest in the city. We don't have it. I'm a single mom.

Austin Bouchard, Ward 2: Tonight is not merely a budget vote. It is a test of principle. For months, this chamber has debated the size of the bill while refusing to confront the failures that produced it. The evidence is everywhere, if this chamber would only consent to see it, the schools. Manchester has declining enrollment, rising spending, and academic returns that remain unacceptable. Yet the district remains committed to Common Core and the costly architecture beneath it. Coachs, interventions, support systems, staffing layers as though complexity itself were achievement. The question is not whether taxpayers should be continuing to fund the model. The question is why this government refuses to question the model at all. The same refusal appears in the facilities; the district's own prior studies raise questions about under-used buildings, yet phase one moves forward with additions to underfilled middle schools and a new Beech Street school this city does not need and cannot afford. That is not reform. That is construction in the place of courage. And beneath it all is a broader direction of the district. Community schools, wraparound services, rolling lunch debt, and expanding non-academic obligations layered on top of education itself. Manchester is not being asked to fund education alone. It is being asked to fund an expanding theory of government that has not proven its results, disclosed its full costs, or justified its destination. The same is true of homelessness. Manchester has not merely responded to homelessness; it has turned emergency into institution. Shelters, encampment cleanups, police calls, fire calls, public work hours, strained neighborhoods, and citywide costs pushed onto residents. Where is the full accounting? Not the line item; the whole cost. What financial obligation does the Manchester taxpayer have to permanently fund services for people who are not from this community, but came here because Manchester made itself the landing place for failures of other communities and systems? That is not cruelty. That is the question responsible government must ask itself before it reaches into the homes of its own people. We are told this is compassion, but compassion without accounting is sentimentality. Compassion that depends on legal force is coercion. If a resident cannot pay, the city can place a lien on the home. Do not call that mercy. This is bad governance wearing a halo. And now public safety is asked to carry the weight. I want a fully staffed police department as much as anybody else. Visible, active, accountable, transparent, trusted and free to enforce order. But residents have been told before more money would close the ranks. The taxpayer has carried the burden before and still vacancies endure. So, before the city converts hope into appropriation, it must ask the question it has evaded. What precisely is different this time? Is crisis the only compensation? Or have we built a city that consumes the very servants it praises? Teachers, police officers, firefighters and public works employees are being asked to carry accumulated weight of civic disorder, social failures this government has refused to confront honestly. Love for Manchester is not measured by one's willingness to fund every failure. It is measured by the courage to tell the truth while there is still time to change course. Do not ask Manchester to finance your refusal to reform. Do not mistake legal power to raise taxes for the moral authority to do so. No to unreformed systems, no to unanswered questions. Tonight, hold the line. No tax cap override.

Jeannette Lund, Ward 4: I am not in favor of raising the tax cap. I've lived in this city all my life except for 13 years. I'm 72 years old and my income doesn't substantiate my lifestyle, so I have to go out and get a part time job. I came to that reasoning with common sense. Does anybody here on this board have common sense? We have water and sewage bills that are going up for the next three years at 19% rate. The following year is 18%. The prices of food, the prices of gas, everything is going up. We elected you people to sit on this board. It's a privilege for you to do that. Have you forgotten that we pay your paychecks with our taxes? You're supposed to be accountable to us. Do you even care about senior citizens? Did senior citizens get a 10% or 12% increase in Social Security this year? I think not. I ask you, I implore you, to look deep into your heart and your conscience and vote against tax increases to the extent that you're asking for. It's ridiculous and deplorable.

Jane Haigh, Ward 1: I have grandchildren that live in ward two, and I had a great opportunity today to go to the concert at Smyth Road School with the band, the strings ensemble and the third-grade and the fourth-grade chorus. So that was a great way to start the day. I think that the schools here are doing very well. I haven't lived here all this time, but my son in law graduated from Central High School. He's doing very well. And you know, I really appreciate the service all of you are doing here. This is really a no-win situation. I would like to ask you to support the compromise budget. That's also called the community first budget. We have a problem here that taxpayers are on the hook because of budget decisions in Concord and Washington, D.C. I'd like to emphasize it's a compromise that doesn't fully fund the city or the schools. I would hate to have to see kids pay for sports or a failure to provide adequate funding for our teachers or our police or our firefighters. I think you have to keep in mind, I'm a taxpayer, I'm not enthused about paying perhaps an extra $70 a month in taxes. The cost of everything that I have to pay for certainly has gone up because of inflation. But this also applies to all the supplies needed for the schools. And when we talk about streets and potholes, first of all, if we don't keep up with fixing the streets, it's only going to get worse. We're not going to have fewer potholes next year because we don't fill the ones that we have this year. And if anything's going up, it must be the price of asphalt to fill the potholes because that's an oil product. And so, the whole thing is complicated. We're not going to be able to hire new police officers, which we need if we can't match the wages that other towns and cities are paying. And if we refuse to raise their wages, then we're trying to balance the budget on the backs of the policemen and the firefighters and the school teachers who aren't getting the raise that they need to deal with inflation. So, in short, you have a difficult decision, but I urge you to go with the compromise budget, keeping in mind that it is a compromise.

Richard Dichard, West High School: This is my 20th year as a school administrator in the Manchester School District. Currently, I'm the principal and have been for the last ten years at Manchester High School West. I come before you tonight out of deep concern for this city's future, a place that I have dedicated virtually all of my career to in education. My concern is for our learners, and my concern is for the well-being of every citizen who calls Manchester home. I'm just going to throw out some things. We've heard a lot of things tonight. But my understanding is the city has a formula. I guess I have a question for everybody. Have we followed or has this board followed that formula for schools in each of the last two years? I believe the answer to that question is no. Now, a lot of people have said we need an audit. Is the school district spending exorbitant amount of money even though we see a decrease in enrollment? Well, I can tell you, as principal of Manchester High School West, nine out of the last ten years, I will operate my building with less people than I had the year before. That is nine out of ten. Again, I hold myself accountable to the taxpayers of the City of Manchester. When our numbers have to be a certain thing, I take care of that and we respect that. I take it extremely seriously in terms of what's at stake here tonight. Transportation, your honor, you and I, of course we walked two miles both to and from school, uphill both ways in our day. Well, that's going to be on the table tonight, ladies and gentlemen. 55% of the students at Manchester High School West are on free and reduced lunch. On the table tonight is those students will have to pay to play sports. Now, if you follow West sports, you know we've got some teams that are in the running. I know some of you have been to our games and we're on the move. I can assure you that will end. To put it plainly, these cuts are very impactful. They are real and they will hurt kids. What are the root causes? We've heard it tonight; chronic underfunding from the State of New Hampshire leaves Manchester to fill the gap. It's why you all have this decision before you tonight. Rising health care costs for city employees. I just want to also support our Manchester police officers as well. I appreciate your indulgence in over the three minutes. We have got to have a competent police force, a full police force. I understand that's on the table tonight. So please do that as well. I forced my wife to take on our health insurance. I'm doing my part to bring our costs down here in Manchester. The City of Manchester will no longer have to pay health care costs to a certain extent that they have over the last few years. I encourage this board, please, these are our students we're talking about and we are West High.

Victoria Sullivan: I apologize. I had to leave earlier. I work with some of our most vulnerable people in our city, and this budget impacts them the most. I've heard a lot tonight about downshifting from the state. And I will tell you that the City of Manchester has received more funds from the State of New Hampshire now than they have

previously. The meals and rooms tax that you received, $11 million, is a 108% increase over what you received in the past, and your education and special ed funding has increased. I was at a town hall meeting with Jim O'Connell, our school board member, and he was talking about funding as well. I reminded him that a few years back, Manchester received over $20 million more than they were expecting from the state. And I asked him if at that time, somehow the taxpayers got some relief if some money was sent back to them. And he admitted that, no, they actually increased the taxes yet again. So, there is no amount of money that is the magic pot that is going to make this board decide that they're not going to raise taxes on people. I understand that. But we have to mitigate the damage that you're doing to these folks. We talk about the children. We hear it's all about the children. Even with the tax cap budget. I do appreciate Alderman Kantor and Alderman Sapienza for bringing forward their budget. And mayor, your tax cap budget as well. Even that is going to hurt people, but I understand where we're at. That's the best we can do at this time. But when we're talking about investing in the children, what about those families that want to invest in their own children and you decide that you're taking money off of their table? You're deciding that they can't spend as much money on food. You're deciding that they can't buy clothes. They can't afford to play sports. You're making those decisions. You're not letting them invest in their own children. And somehow you think that taking money from those families and giving it to the government and then making those families more reliant on the government is helping them in some way. It's so bizarre to me to listen to this, and it's very disheartening to hear this be called a community first budget. There's no community first in this. There's no community coming together to solve these problems. You're going to the taxpayers and stealing from their kitchen tables. That's what you're doing. If you want community first, what happened to the private and public partnerships that we used to have in this city? $7 million skateboard park. Why aren't the businesses paying for that? $2 million downtown sidewalk that doesn't need to be repaired when, by the way, the one right here on the corner has a piece of metal sticking out of it that I tripped over coming in tonight. But we're not going to address the problems that we have with sidewalks. We're going to rip up the pretty one because somebody's got a partial grant and didn't care that that's going to put the taxpayers on the hook for the other $1.5 million of it. So, there are serious problems that we have in this city and right now, with the tax cap. The community first tax cap budget, it puts community first, I guess all the organizations that you're going to fund, but it doesn't put the families first. And then we're going to have more families that owe more for lunches and put a bigger burden on the taxpayers because they can't afford to feed their families. It shouldn't be community first. It should be taxpayers and families first budget that you put forward tonight.

Avery Cyr, Ward 3: I just wanted to quickly say, as someone who's run for alderman of ward three and got 45% of the vote, I think there's a lot of people in ward three that would be heartbroken if there were any cuts made to the school district. And that's all that I have to say on that.
